headline: Germany's medical cannabis imports nearly tripled to 201 tonnes in 2025
dek: Imports into Germany rose about 176% in 2025 and UK pharmacy items hit 1.7 million, but a Blossom Pharma chief warns volume is outrunning profit into 2027.
key_points: Germany imported about 201 tonnes of medical cannabis flower and extract in 2025, up from about 73 tonnes in 2024, according to figures in a Business of Cannabis guest column.
Canada and Portugal supplied almost three quarters of that volume, about 93 and 55 tonnes respectively.
In England, about 1.7 million privately prescribed unlicensed cannabis items were dispensed in 2025, up from about 669,000, and UK flower imports doubled to about 30 tonnes.
The author, Blossom Pharma's chief executive, says German wholesale prices fell about 26% in a year and expects 2027 to reward consistent, well-documented suppliers.
body: Europe's two largest medical cannabis markets are taking in far more product than a year ago, and paying less for it. Germany imported about 201.1 tonnes of medical and scientific cannabis, flower and extracts together, in 2025, up from about 72.9 tonnes in 2024, a rise of roughly 176%. The figures appear in a guest column published by Business of Cannabis on 18 November, which attributes them to the 2026 statistical report of ABDA, the German pharmacists' federation, drawing on data from the federal drug agency BfArM.

The author, Oskar Fletcher, is chief executive of Blossom Pharma, a pharmaceutical contract manufacturer that supplies European markets, so the piece is an industry view rather than independent reporting. Its numbers are still the clearest snapshot yet of how far the German medical market has grown under its medical cannabis law, the MedCanG. A note of caution: Business of Cannabis's own homepage cites a slightly different BfArM total of about 205 tonnes for 2025, against about 72.9 tonnes in 2024. Either way, imports roughly tripled.

Two countries dominate. According to the table cited in the column, Canada shipped about 93 tonnes to Germany in 2025 and Portugal about 55.2 tonnes, together almost 74% of the total. The author notes that trade figures show where product was shipped from, not necessarily where it was grown. By these figures, Canada alone supplied close to half of Germany's medical cannabis imports in 2025.

BfArM's own import pages confirm the legal route, though not the totals: importing cannabis for medical or scientific use requires a permit under section 4 of Germany's medical cannabis law, and the agency publishes its import volumes as charts by quarter and by country of origin.
> Europe is buying three times the cannabis it did, but the price per gram is doing the opposite.
## The UK is growing faster from a smaller base

In the United Kingdom, imports of unlicensed cannabis flower reached about 30.1 tonnes in 2025, double the 15 tonnes of 2024, based on Business of Cannabis analysis of Home Office information. In England, community pharmacies dispensed about 1.7 million privately prescribed unlicensed cannabis items in 2025, up from about 669,000 the year before, based on its analysis of NHS Business Services Authority data. By our calculation that is an increase of about 154%. The column notes that items are not patients, and that the count includes products other than flower.

That is the market the high-street pharmacy chain Boots entered with its SureLeaf service on 16 November, as we reported. It also leaves UK patients exposed to supply shocks: when the Dutch grower Bedrocan collapsed this month, it strained supply in both the UK and Italy, as we reported on 9 November.

The column's central warning is about margins. Fletcher writes that average wholesale prices in Germany fell about 26% over the past 12 months on a comparable-product basis. That figure is Blossom's own observation, not a published dataset. He says Blossom's flower shipments to European markets rose about 35% across the same period, so volume is up while the price per gram is down.

His forecast for 2027 follows from that. He expects volume growth to outpace financial performance; repeat orders to matter more than headline import totals; continued price pressure on interchangeable flower, with wider gaps between product segments; and supplier qualification and documentation, including EU-GMP processing, to become a sharper commercial dividing line. He also argues Europe should be planned country by country, that working capital and cash discipline will matter more, and that buyers will concentrate repeat business with fewer, more consistent suppliers. He describes himself as optimistic.

For Canadian and Portuguese exporters, the German numbers confirm demand but not pricing power. A market that tripled while wholesale prices fell by about a quarter rewards scale and reliability, not novelty. For UK distributors, a market growing faster than Germany's in percentage terms, but still at about a seventh of its import volume, looks like the next place where price pressure will arrive.

The deals already reflect that. As we reported on 17 November, Curaleaf's UK laboratory agreed to manufacture and distribute products from Canada's PURPLEFARM for British patients, a sign that producers want a local, licensed partner that can carry documentation and supply through the UK system.

Watch BfArM's next quarterly import chart for whether 2026 volumes keep climbing or level off. Watch German policy on telemedicine prescriptions, which could cut demand if tightened. And watch NHS Business Services Authority data for 2026, which will show whether the UK's 2025 surge continued.
